progress: Reading the change — VAT moves from one rate for the invoice to a rate per line.
Working out what the new rounding does to invoices that already exist.
The arithmetic is right; the rule it implements is a question for someone else. Writing that.

review.summary:
An invoice with mixed VAT rates — 20% on goods, 5% on the installation line — took the *first* line's rate and applied it to the whole net. On the invoice the Leeds branch reported, that came out £38 too high.

VAT is now computed per line and summed, with each line rounded to the nearest penny on the way. A new `lineVat` does the per-line maths and `roundMinor` does the rounding, halves away from zero. A test covers an invoice carrying two rates.

chapters.title: VAT per line, rounded per line
chapters.explanation: `lineVat` computes and rounds one line's VAT; `invoiceTotals` sums those instead of applying one rate to the whole net. The rounding rule is new and applies to every invoice, not just mixed-rate ones.

chapters.title: The mixed-rate test
chapters.explanation: Two lines at 20% and 5% on a £20 net, expecting £2.50 of VAT. It pins the reported bug; it does not pin the rounding.

comments.body:
Rounding halves away from zero is a choice, and it is not obviously the one the rule wants.

HMRC lets a trader round VAT down to the nearest penny per line, or round to the nearest penny, as long as it is applied consistently — and whichever this is now, it is what every invoice gets from here on. A one-line comment naming the rule being implemented, and who confirmed it, would make this reviewable by the person who actually knows.

Invoices that already exist will re-render with a different total.

Rounding each line and then summing can differ from rounding once at the end by up to half a penny per line. Anything that re-computes totals from stored lines — a PDF regenerated, a credit note, the statement view — will now disagree with the figure the customer was sent and paid. Worth knowing whether those paths recompute or read a stored total before this ships.

verdict.reasoning:
The arithmetic does what the description says; what I can't settle is whether the rounding rule it introduces is the right one.

- **Checked the maths** — 20% of £10 plus 5% of £10 is £2.50, and the new test asserts exactly that. The old code would have returned £4.00 here, which matches the reported symptom.
- **Read the rounding** — `Math.sign(v) * Math.round(Math.abs(v))` is round-half-away-from-zero, which differs from `Math.round` only on negative halves. Credit notes carry negative lines, so it does come up.
- **Couldn't settle the rule** — per-line versus whole-invoice rounding is a tax decision, not a code one, and nothing in the diff says which one the business follows. Someone who knows the answer should say so before this ships.
- **Couldn't check the re-render paths** — whether stored invoices recompute their totals is outside this diff and there is no checkout here. That is the risk that decides whether this is safe to release quietly.
- **No blockers** — nothing here is wrong on its own terms, so this is a question rather than a refusal.
